title: Isomorphic Groups
short: An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism; to show two groups are not isomorphic, find a property one has and the other lacks: order, being abelian or cyclic, or how many elements have each order.
trouble: Students conclude two groups are isomorphic because they have the same order, or that none exists because one map they tried failed.

blocks.html: Two groups can look different on paper and be the same group in disguise: $U(10)$ and $\mathbb{Z}_{4}$ have the same multiplication pattern once you rename the elements. An isomorphism is such a renaming.

Definition. An isomorphism is a homomorphism that is a bijection. If one exists, $G$ and $H$ are isomorphic, $G \cong H$. The inverse of an isomorphism is again a homomorphism, so $\cong$ is an equivalence relation. By the kernel test, a homomorphism is one-to-one exactly when its kernel is trivial.
Write down a map and check the two conditions: it is a homomorphism, and it is a bijection (for finite groups of the same order, one-to-one is enough, and that is the kernel test).

Theorem. Every cyclic group of order $n$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$.
Proof. Let $G = \langle a \rangle$ with $|a| = n$, and define $\psi: \mathbb{Z}_{n} \to G$ by $\psi(k) = a^{k}$. It is well defined, because $a^{k} = a^{j}$ exactly when $k \equiv j \pmod n$ (the order lemma). It is a homomorphism: $\psi(j + k) = a^{j+k} = a^{j}a^{k}$. Its kernel is $\{k : a^{k} = e\} = \{0\}$, so it is one-to-one, and since both groups have $n$ elements it is onto. $\square$ The same argument shows every infinite cyclic group is $\cong \mathbb{Z}$.

blocks.title: $U(10) \cong \mathbb{Z}_{4}$
steps: It is a bijection, and $3^{j + k} = 3^{j}3^{k}$ turns addition mod 4 into multiplication mod 10.

blocks.text: Showing two groups are not isomorphic

blocks.html: Find a property that isomorphisms preserve and that one group has and the other lacks. Isomorphisms preserve the order of the group, the order of each element (so the number of elements of each order), being abelian, being cyclic, and the size of the center. Trying one map and watching it fail proves nothing: some other map might work.

steps: $D_{4}$ has five elements of order 2 (four reflections and $r^{2}$); $Q_{8}$ has one ($-1$).
blocks.a: Different counts of elements by order.

blocks.html: Concluding "isomorphic" from equal orders: $\mathbb{Z}_{6}$ and $S_{3}$ both have six elements, but one is abelian and the other is not. And concluding "not isomorphic" because one map failed: the map $\mathbb{Z}_{4} \to U(10)$, $k \mapsto 7^{k}$, also works, while $k \mapsto 9^{k}$ does not; only a property that no isomorphism could change settles "no".

An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism, a renaming that keeps the table. Every cyclic group of order $n$ is $\cong \mathbb{Z}_{n}$. To show $G \not\cong H$, find an invariant that differs, such as the number of elements of some order.
